prompt: Consider the claim: "If $x^2 = 36$, then $x = 6$." Give a value of $x$ that is a counterexample.
hint: You need a number that makes the "if" part true while making the "then" part false.

hints.text: You need a number that makes the "if" part true while making the "then" part false.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Try an easier claim: "If $x^2 = 4$, then $x = 2$" is broken by $x = -2$, since $(-2)^2 = 4$ but $-2 \ne 2$. Pull the same trick on $36$.
What other number, besides 6, squares to 36?
$x = -6$: it satisfies $(-6)^2 = 36$, but it is not equal to 6.

explanation: A counterexample must satisfy the hypothesis and break the conclusion.
The conclusion fails because $-6 \ne 6$. So $-6$ is a counterexample and the claim is false.
The repaired statement would be "if $x^2 = 36$, then $x = 6$ or $x = -6$."

alternativeExplanations.title: Squaring erases the sign
steps: Multiplying two negatives gives a positive, so a negative number squares to the same value its positive twin does.
Every "square equals" claim therefore has two solutions — the positive one and the negative one you almost forgot.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: The common wrong move is answering 6 — but 6 makes the statement TRUE, so it is an example, not a counterexample.

A counterexample has to obey the "if" and break the "then." Ask both questions about your candidate: "Does it square to 36?" ($-6$: yes) and "Does it dodge being 6?" ($-6$: yes). That is what makes $-6$ the answer.
